metadata.title: Cloud Computing — Full Relationship-Rich Semantic Knowledge Graph
metadata.purpose: A detailed graph of cloud-computing concepts, service models, architecture, dependencies, providers, economics, operations, security, privacy, standards, history, and legal context.
metadata.source_policy: The supplied Simple English Wikipedia extract is authoritative for source-derived claims. Modern provider and architecture concepts are marked as synthesis. No external web research was performed.
metadata.temporal_caveat: Provider/product examples in the article are historical. They are preserved as source-era examples, not as a current market ranking.
metadata.provenance_policy: Line numbers refer to the extracted source lines. Empty line lists identify concepts added as explanatory synthesis.

schema.graph_design: Directed typed relationships express mechanisms, dependencies, roles, constraints, examples, and distinctions rather than generic related_to links.

nodes.label: Cloud computing
nodes.description: Computing services delivered by an external or managed provider and accessed over a network, including storage, processing, platforms, and applications.

nodes.label: The cloud
nodes.description: A metaphor for the Internet and for components and services managed by others; the abstraction hides underlying complexity.

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.description: The network through which cloud services are commonly accessed.

nodes.label: Computing service
nodes.description: A computing capability delivered as a service rather than solely as locally owned infrastructure.

nodes.label: Compute resource
nodes.description: Processing capacity made available to workloads.

nodes.label: Storage resource
nodes.description: Capacity for storing data, offered as a service.

nodes.label: Development environment
nodes.description: A development environment that can be consumed without owning all underlying infrastructure.

nodes.label: Electricity utility analogy
nodes.description: The source compares cloud computing to electricity: consumers use the utility without managing its production and delivery infrastructure.

nodes.label: Data center
nodes.description: A facility containing computing and storage infrastructure from which cloud services are delivered.

nodes.label: Cloud infrastructure
nodes.description: Underlying compute, network, and storage resources used to deliver cloud services.

nodes.label: Virtualization
nodes.description: Abstraction of physical resources into logical computing environments and resource pools.

nodes.label: Network
nodes.description: Connectivity that enables clients, services, and distributed components to communicate.

nodes.label: Application programming interface (API)
nodes.description: An interface through which cloud components expose functionality and communicate.

nodes.label: Web service
nodes.description: A network-accessible software interface for machine-to-machine interaction.

nodes.label: Cloud consumer / user
nodes.description: A person or organization that consumes cloud services.

nodes.label: Cloud provider
nodes.description: An organization that owns and operates cloud systems for others.

nodes.label: Cloud vendor
nodes.description: A company that sells products and services enabling cloud delivery, adoption, or use.

nodes.label: Cloud architect
nodes.description: A person designing cloud software-system architecture, often working for a cloud integrator.

nodes.label: Cloud integrator
nodes.description: An organization or role integrating cloud components and systems.

nodes.label: Service-level agreement (SLA)
nodes.description: A commercial agreement describing service quality or availability commitments.

nodes.label: Quality of service
nodes.description: Service-performance requirements that cloud offerings may need to meet.

nodes.label: Open standards
nodes.description: Public specifications and interfaces that support interoperability and ecosystem growth.

nodes.label: Open-source software
nodes.description: Software whose source is available under a license permitting defined forms of use and modification.

nodes.label: Utility computing
nodes.description: Measured consumption of compute or storage resources, commonly billed by usage like a traditional utility.

nodes.label: Grid computing
nodes.description: Distributed computing in which loosely coupled networked computers cooperate on large tasks.

nodes.label: Autonomic computing
nodes.description: Computer systems capable of managing themselves to some degree.

nodes.label: Distributed computing
nodes.description: Work performed across multiple connected machines.

nodes.label: Peer-to-peer networking
nodes.description: An architecture in which peers share resources or communicate without every operation depending on one central service.

nodes.label: Centralization
nodes.description: Concentration of infrastructure, management, or data operations in coordinated systems or sites.

nodes.label: Multitenancy
nodes.description: Multiple consumers share underlying resources while remaining logically separated by the service design.

nodes.label: Scalability
nodes.description: The ability to adjust capacity to changing demand.

nodes.label: Elasticity
nodes.description: The ability to provision or release resources as demand changes.

nodes.label: Reliability
nodes.description: The ability of a service to operate consistently and recover from failures.

nodes.label: Redundancy
nodes.description: Duplicated components or sites that reduce the impact of individual failures.

nodes.label: Availability
nodes.description: The proportion of time a service is usable.

nodes.label: Disaster recovery
nodes.description: Procedures and capabilities for restoring service and data after disruption.

nodes.label: Business continuity
nodes.description: Maintaining critical operations through outages or disruptions.

nodes.label: Performance
nodes.description: Observed responsiveness and capacity of a cloud service.

nodes.label: Network bandwidth
nodes.description: The capacity of a network path to carry data.

nodes.label: Network latency
nodes.description: Time for a request or data to travel through a network and be processed.

nodes.label: Resource utilization
nodes.description: The fraction of available capacity being used.

nodes.label: Peak load
nodes.description: A period of unusually high demand.

nodes.label: Capital expenditure (CapEx)
nodes.description: Up-front spending to buy infrastructure.

nodes.label: Operational expenditure (OpEx)
nodes.description: Ongoing costs of consuming or operating services.

nodes.label: Pay-as-you-go billing
nodes.description: Charges tied to measured resource consumption.

nodes.label: Subscription billing
nodes.description: Recurring charges for a service or entitlement.

nodes.label: Shared resource pool
nodes.description: A pool of resources shared across consumers to improve utilization and flexibility.

nodes.label: Device and location independence
nodes.description: Access from different locations and devices, subject to connectivity and access rules.

nodes.label: Sustainability
nodes.description: Reducing resource waste and environmental impact through efficient infrastructure and operations.

nodes.label: Cloud security
nodes.description: Protection of infrastructure, identities, applications, and data against unauthorized access or disruption.

nodes.label: Cloud privacy
nodes.description: Rules and practices governing access to, use of, and disclosure of data handled by providers.

nodes.label: Data sovereignty and jurisdiction
nodes.description: Legal and regulatory questions arising when cloud data or infrastructure crosses national borders.

nodes.label: Vendor lock-in
nodes.description: Dependence on provider-specific services or interfaces that makes migration costly.

nodes.label: Cloud outage
nodes.description: An event in which a cloud service becomes unavailable or degraded.

nodes.label: Audit log
nodes.description: A record of accesses or actions; customer access to provider logs may be limited.

nodes.label: Data
nodes.description: Information stored, processed, transmitted, or synchronized by cloud systems.

nodes.label: Metadata
nodes.description: Data describing other data or storage objects.

nodes.label: Cloud client
nodes.description: Hardware or software relying on cloud services for application delivery or other capabilities.

nodes.label: Web browser
nodes.description: A client application used to access cloud applications and services.

nodes.label: Thin client
nodes.description: A client that relies heavily on remote cloud services.

nodes.label: Thick client
nodes.description: A richer local client, such as a browser, that can access cloud services.

nodes.label: Cloud application
nodes.description: An application delivered through cloud infrastructure, often reducing local installation and maintenance.

nodes.label: Web application
nodes.description: An application accessed through web technologies, commonly via a browser.

nodes.label: Software as a Service (SaaS)
nodes.description: Software hosted and operated by a provider and accessed over a network.

nodes.label: Platform as a Service (PaaS)
nodes.description: A platform or solution stack delivered as a service so developers can deploy applications without managing all underlying layers.

nodes.label: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
nodes.description: Compute, storage, networking, and related infrastructure delivered as a service.

nodes.label: Software plus services
nodes.description: A model combining software with provider-hosted online services.

nodes.label: Cloud storage
nodes.description: Data storage delivered as a service, often billed by capacity and time.

nodes.label: Cloud database
nodes.description: A managed or hosted database-like service consumed over a network.

nodes.label: Storage synchronization
nodes.description: Keeping data synchronized across devices or services.

nodes.label: Object storage
nodes.description: A storage service exposing data as objects, commonly through an API.

nodes.label: Network-attached storage (NAS)
nodes.description: Storage made available to systems over a network.

nodes.label: Cloud management
nodes.description: Tools and processes for provisioning, monitoring, and managing cloud resources.

nodes.label: Identity service
nodes.description: A service handling identities, authentication, or authorization.

nodes.label: Integration service
nodes.description: A service connecting applications or components, such as queues or messaging.

nodes.label: Mapping service
nodes.description: A network-accessible mapping capability.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.description: A service supporting online payment processing.

nodes.label: Search service
nodes.description: A hosted search capability.

nodes.label: Crowd-work service
nodes.description: A service distributing tasks to a pool of people or participants.

nodes.label: Virtualization environment
nodes.description: A logical environment abstracting underlying physical servers or resources.

nodes.label: Full virtualization
nodes.description: A virtualization approach exposing a sufficiently complete hardware interface.

nodes.label: Paravirtualization
nodes.description: A virtualization approach using guest/hypervisor cooperation and specialized interfaces.

nodes.label: Resource metering
nodes.description: Measuring resource consumption for billing or capacity management.

nodes.label: Resource provisioning
nodes.description: Allocating resources and making them available to consumers.

nodes.label: Monitoring
nodes.description: Collecting and evaluating performance or health information.

nodes.label: Application development
nodes.description: Creating, testing, deploying, and maintaining applications on cloud platforms.

nodes.label: Data portability
nodes.description: The ability to move data between systems or providers.

nodes.label: Interoperability
nodes.description: Different components or systems exchange information through compatible interfaces and standards.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.description: A web protocol listed among cloud communication standards.

nodes.label: XMPP
nodes.description: A communications protocol listed among cloud communication standards.

nodes.label: OAuth
nodes.description: An authorization framework listed under security standards and identity services.

nodes.label: OpenID
nodes.description: An identity-related standard or protocol named by the source.

nodes.label: SSL/TLS
nodes.description: Cryptographic protocols listed among cloud security standards.

nodes.label: Atom syndication
nodes.description: A syndication format listed in the source's standards section.

nodes.label: AJAX
nodes.description: A browser-side web technology named under client standards.

nodes.label: HTML5 offline capabilities
nodes.description: Offline capabilities listed under client standards.

nodes.label: Open Virtualization Format (OVF)
nodes.description: A virtualization format listed under infrastructure standards.

nodes.label: LAMP stack
nodes.description: A solution stack named under platform standards.

nodes.label: Space-based architecture
nodes.description: An architecture pattern listed as a platform solution-stack example.

nodes.label: XML
nodes.description: A structured data format listed by the source.

nodes.label: JSON
nodes.description: A structured data format listed by the source.

nodes.label: REST
nodes.description: A web-service architecture style listed by the source.

nodes.label: Political and geopolitical issues
nodes.description: Cloud services cross borders and encounter different legal regimes and government-access rules.

nodes.label: Legal issues
nodes.description: Cloud delivery raises issues involving licensing, trademarks, contracts, data protection, and jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Affero General Public License (AGPL)
nodes.description: A license described as addressing a perceived loophole for modified software run over a network.

nodes.label: Internal cloud provider
nodes.description: An organization provides cloud-like services internally to itself.

nodes.label: Public cloud
nodes.description: Cloud services offered by a provider to external consumers.

nodes.label: Private cloud
nodes.description: Cloud infrastructure dedicated to one organization.

nodes.label: Hybrid cloud
nodes.description: A combination of cloud and other environments.

nodes.label: Cloud region
nodes.description: A geographic deployment area used to place infrastructure near customers or address local requirements.

nodes.label: Local infrastructure deployment
nodes.description: Deploying infrastructure in a selected country or region.

nodes.label: Shared-responsibility security model
nodes.description: Provider and customer security duties vary by service model.

nodes.label: Access control
nodes.description: Rules defining who can access resources or perform actions.

nodes.label: Encryption
nodes.description: Cryptographic transformation protecting data confidentiality.

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.description: A retained copy of data used for recovery after loss or corruption.

nodes.label: Cloud migration
nodes.description: Moving applications, data, and operations between environments or providers.

nodes.label: Billing and management overhead
nodes.description: The systems and work needed to meter usage, manage resources, and charge consumers.

nodes.label: Capacity planning
nodes.description: Estimating resources needed to meet workload demand.

nodes.label: Resource efficiency
nodes.description: Delivering useful work with less wasted infrastructure and energy.

nodes.label: Data residency
nodes.description: The location where data is stored or processed.

nodes.label: Government access to data
nodes.description: The possibility of lawful or contested government access to provider-held information.

nodes.label: Webmail

nodes.label: Contact-list synchronization

nodes.label: Additional contemporary provider context
nodes.description: Additional providers below are included as broad industry context, not as claims from the supplied article.

nodes.label: Oracle Cloud
nodes.description: A major provider in broader industry context; not named in the supplied article.

nodes.label: Alibaba Cloud
nodes.description: A major provider in broader industry context; not named in the supplied article.

nodes.label: Cloudflare

nodes.label: DigitalOcean
nodes.description: A cloud infrastructure provider in broader industry context; not named in the supplied article.

nodes.label: Provider comparison dimensions
nodes.description: Providers can be compared by compute, storage, platforms, networking, regions, pricing, compliance, and service dependencies.

nodes.label: Managed-service dependency
nodes.description: Applications may depend on provider-specific databases, queues, identity, storage APIs, and monitoring systems.

nodes.label: Portability versus managed-service depth
nodes.description: Provider-native managed services reduce operational burden but may increase coupling to provider APIs and behavior.

nodes.label: Multi-cloud architecture
nodes.description: An architecture using services from more than one provider; it adds options but also integration and operational complexity.

nodes.label: Cloud networking
nodes.description: Virtual networks, routing, DNS, gateways, load balancing, and connectivity link cloud components and clients.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.description: Distributes requests or connections across multiple backend instances.

nodes.label: Domain Name System (DNS)
nodes.description: Resolves names to network destinations used to reach cloud endpoints.

nodes.label: Content delivery network (CDN)
nodes.description: Caches or serves content from distributed edge locations.

nodes.label: Container
nodes.description: A packaged application process and dependencies isolated using operating-system-level mechanisms.

nodes.label: Virtual machine (VM)
nodes.description: A software-defined machine running on virtualized compute infrastructure.

nodes.label: Workload orchestration
nodes.description: Schedules and manages application workloads across compute resources.

nodes.label: Kubernetes
nodes.description: A common container orchestration platform; not named in the supplied article.

nodes.label: Observability
nodes.description: Logs, metrics, traces, and signals used to understand service behavior.

nodes.label: Identity and access management (IAM)
nodes.description: Controls identities, permissions, and access to cloud resources.

nodes.label: Key management service
nodes.description: Manages cryptographic keys used to protect cloud data and services.

nodes.label: Managed database
nodes.description: A provider-operated database service abstracting installation, patching, backups, and some availability tasks.

nodes.label: Message queue
nodes.description: A buffering and asynchronous communication service; SQS is the source's example.

nodes.label: Object store
nodes.description: A scalable storage service accessed through an API; S3 is the source's example.

nodes.label: Secrets management
nodes.description: Stores and distributes credentials, tokens, and other secrets to authorized workloads.

nodes.label: Compliance controls
nodes.description: Requirements and evidence related to legal, regulatory, contractual, and industry obligations.

nodes.label: Cloud cost management
nodes.description: Budgeting, allocating, observing, and optimizing cloud consumption and billing.

nodes.label: Data egress cost
nodes.description: Costs or constraints associated with transferring data out of a provider environment.

nodes.label: Migration complexity
nodes.description: Effort involved in moving applications, data, identity, networking, and managed-service dependencies.

nodes.label: Cloud service dependency graph
nodes.description: A map of dependencies among applications, compute, networks, identity, storage, databases, queues, monitoring, and provider services.

nodes.label: Cloud control plane
nodes.description: Interfaces and services used to provision and manage resources.

nodes.label: Cloud data plane
nodes.description: Components that process user traffic and application data.

nodes.label: Shared-responsibility model
nodes.description: Security responsibilities are divided between provider and customer according to service model and contract.

nodes.label: Autoscaling
nodes.description: Automatically adjusts resource capacity in response to demand or policy.

nodes.label: Health check
nodes.description: A probe used to determine whether a component can serve requests.

nodes.label: Failover
nodes.description: Redirecting service to healthy redundant capacity after a failure.

nodes.label: Data replication
nodes.description: Maintaining copies of data across nodes or sites.

nodes.label: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
nodes.description: Defining and managing infrastructure through versioned machine-readable configuration.

nodes.label: CI/CD
nodes.description: Automated integration, testing, and delivery/deployment of software changes.

nodes.label: Incident response
nodes.description: Detection, triage, containment, and recovery for service or security incidents.

nodes.label: Availability zone
nodes.description: A fault-isolated location within a cloud region; provider terminology varies.

nodes.label: Edge computing
nodes.description: Computing near users, devices, or data sources rather than only in centralized data centers.

nodes.label: Cloud financial operations (FinOps)
nodes.description: Practice aligning cloud spending, engineering choices, and business value.

nodes.label: Data classification
nodes.description: Labeling data by sensitivity and handling requirements.

nodes.label: Identity federation
nodes.description: Using trusted identity relationships to authenticate users across systems.

nodes.label: Service mesh
nodes.description: Infrastructure for managing service-to-service communication, security, and telemetry.

nodes.label: Microservices architecture
nodes.description: An application architecture built from independently deployable services.

nodes.label: Serverless computing
nodes.description: A cloud model that abstracts server management and commonly scales execution based on requests or events.

nodes.label: Function as a Service (FaaS)
nodes.description: A serverless pattern running functions in response to events or invocations.

nodes.label: Event-driven architecture
nodes.description: Components communicate through events or messages.

nodes.label: Provider-specific API
nodes.description: An API unique to or strongly associated with a cloud provider's services.

nodes.label: Cloud-native design
nodes.description: Designing applications for automation, distributed services, managed infrastructure, and failure-aware operations.

nodes.label: Cloud economies of scale
nodes.description: Shared infrastructure can spread fixed costs across many consumers; this is explanatory synthesis beyond the source's exact wording.

formal_models.name: Cloud service abstraction
formal_models.description: Provider-operated infrastructure is abstracted through virtualization and service interfaces so consumers can use capabilities without managing every physical detail.

formal_models.name: Service-model stack
formal_models.description: IaaS exposes infrastructure; PaaS exposes a platform; SaaS exposes an application. Provider responsibility generally increases at higher abstraction levels.

formal_models.name: Typical cloud application dependency graph
formal_models.description: Illustrative modern dependency chain; not every component is explicitly discussed in the source.

formal_models.name: Usage and cost
formal_models.description: Measured consumption supports usage billing and cost visibility; total cost still depends on usage and pricing.

formal_models.name: Reliability and recovery
formal_models.description: Redundancy, replication, backups, failover, and tested recovery can reduce failure impact but do not guarantee zero downtime or data loss.

formal_models.name: Cloud security responsibility
formal_models.description: Provider and consumer responsibilities vary by service model; identity, access, encryption, and compliance remain key concerns.

formal_models.name: Architecture and interoperability
formal_models.description: Cloud components communicate through APIs and web services; compatible interfaces can improve interoperability.

formal_models.name: Provider lock-in and portability
formal_models.description: Managed services reduce operational burden but may create provider-specific dependencies that increase migration effort.

formal_models.name: Data jurisdiction
formal_models.description: Global cloud deployments cross legal borders; region, data handling, contracts, and applicable law influence compliance.

formal_models.name: History described by the source
formal_models.description: The article traces utility-computing ideas to 1960, cloud terminology to the early 1990s, AWS access in 2002, and wider research/mainstream attention in 2007–2008.

source_claims.claim: Cloud computing provides externally managed services such as storage, computing power, and development environments.
The article compares cloud computing to electricity utilities and describes pay-for-use consumption.
Cloud computing is related to but distinct from grid, utility, and autonomic computing.
The source describes cloud infrastructure as data-center services built on compute and storage virtualization.
SLAs, open standards, and open-source software are identified as important to cloud service delivery and growth.
Multitenancy and shared resource pools can improve utilization and reduce the need to engineer for peak load.
The article describes location independence, scalability, redundant-site reliability, and possible performance/outage limitations.
The article raises privacy concerns because providers may access, alter, delete, or disclose cloud-held data under policy or law.
The source names Google, Amazon/AWS, Yahoo!, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, HP, and SAP among providers or traditional vendors.
The source attributes a public-utility vision of computation to John McCarthy in 1960.
The source says Amazon opened access to its systems through AWS in 2002 on a utility-computing basis.
The source describes increased cloud research in 2007 and mainstream attention by mid-2008.
The article discusses geopolitical and legal issues arising from cross-border cloud services.
The source lists application, client, infrastructure, platform, service, and storage as cloud component categories.
The article lists HTTP, XMPP, OAuth, OpenID, SSL/TLS, Atom, AJAX, HTML5 offline, OVF, LAMP, XML, JSON, and REST among standards or technologies.
The article describes AGPL as addressing a perceived loophole for modified free software run over a network.
Provider and product examples in the article are historical and should not be interpreted as a current market ranking.
Additional contemporary providers and modern architecture dependencies in this graph are labeled as synthesis, not as claims from the supplied article.

semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: A cloud may use grid techniques, but the terms are not synonyms.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Service abstraction versus measured consumption and billing.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Usage billing alone does not define cloud computing.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Service delivery versus systems capable of self-management.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Automation can be a characteristic but is not the entire cloud model.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Operating cloud systems versus selling enabling products or services.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: An organization can play both roles, but responsibilities differ.
The model changes which layers the consumer operates.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Application deployment platform versus hosted application.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Building on a platform differs from consuming finished software.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Changing capacity versus consistent operation and failure handling.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: A scalable system can still experience outages.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Historical examples versus a current market comparison.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: The source does not establish present-day market share or provider quality.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Operational abstraction versus coupling to provider-specific APIs and behavior.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Managed services trade operational work against migration flexibility.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Physical/jurisdictional location versus legal authority and rules.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Choosing a region does not alone resolve all legal duties.

semantic_distinctions.difference: Protection of systems/data versus rules governing use, access, retention, and disclosure.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Security controls do not answer every privacy question.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud computing is just another name for the Internet.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: The cloud is a metaphor; cloud computing describes services delivered using networks and managed systems.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud computing and grid computing mean the same thing.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Grid computing is distributed computation; cloud computing is a service-delivery model that may use distributed infrastructure.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Every cloud service is billed only by usage.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: The source says many services use utility billing while others use subscriptions.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud computing eliminates all infrastructure costs and operations work.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: It shifts some ownership to providers, but consumers still manage workloads, access, configuration, costs, and data.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud scalability means outages cannot happen.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Scalability and reliability are different properties; cloud services can still fail.
Centralization may provide specialist controls but also concentrates sensitive data and control.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: The provider can never access customer data.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: The supplied article explicitly raises provider access, alteration, deletion, and disclosure concerns.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Provider names in the source represent today's leading-provider ranking.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: The source contains historical examples and is not a current market ranking.
Cross-border services raise jurisdiction, residency, privacy, and legal questions.
Open standards help interoperability, but provider-specific services and operations may still complicate migration.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Multi-cloud automatically reduces cost and complexity.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Multi-cloud adds integration and operations work even when it offers choice.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: A backup alone proves disaster recovery works.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Recovery depends on backup integrity, retention, restoration procedures, and testing.

review_questions.question: Define cloud computing.
review_questions.answer: A model where storage, processing, platforms, or applications are delivered by an external or managed provider and accessed over a network.

review_questions.question: What does the electricity analogy explain?
review_questions.answer: Consumers use a utility without managing how it is produced and delivered.

review_questions.question: How does grid computing differ?
review_questions.answer: Grid computing distributes tasks across loosely coupled computers; cloud computing is a service-delivery model.

review_questions.question: What is utility computing?
review_questions.answer: Measured compute or storage resources billed according to use.

review_questions.question: What is autonomic computing?
review_questions.answer: Systems designed to manage themselves to some degree.

review_questions.question: What is multitenancy?
review_questions.answer: Multiple consumers share underlying resources while being logically separated.

review_questions.question: How can multitenancy improve utilization?
review_questions.answer: Shared resources can serve workloads that would otherwise leave capacity idle.

review_questions.question: Why can cloud reduce peak-load overprovisioning?
review_questions.answer: Consumers can obtain extra capacity from a provider rather than own capacity for every peak.

review_questions.question: What is the difference between IaaS and PaaS?
review_questions.answer: IaaS delivers infrastructure; PaaS delivers a platform/solution stack for deploying applications.

review_questions.question: What does SaaS deliver?
review_questions.answer: A hosted software application.

review_questions.question: What role does virtualization play?
review_questions.answer: It abstracts physical resources into logical environments that can be allocated as services.

review_questions.question: What is an SLA?
review_questions.answer: A service-level agreement specifying service-quality expectations or commitments.

review_questions.question: Does an SLA mean perfect availability?
review_questions.answer: No. Outages can still occur; an SLA defines commitments or remedies.

review_questions.answer: Database-like services, NAS, synchronization, and web/object storage.

review_questions.question: What does the source say about storage metadata?
review_questions.answer: Metadata operations may be centralized while data nodes scale independently.

review_questions.question: Why can bandwidth affect cloud performance?
review_questions.answer: Cloud clients depend on network connectivity; insufficient bandwidth or high network load can degrade response.

review_questions.question: What can redundant sites support?
review_questions.answer: Reliability, business continuity, and disaster recovery.

review_questions.question: What is one limit of redundancy?
review_questions.answer: It does not guarantee uninterrupted service, and customers may have limited control during provider outages.

review_questions.question: Why does cloud raise privacy concerns?
review_questions.answer: Providers may access, alter, delete, or disclose hosted data under policies or legal processes.

review_questions.question: What is data residency?
review_questions.answer: The location where data is stored or processed.

review_questions.question: What is data sovereignty?
review_questions.answer: Legal authority and jurisdiction that apply to data and systems.

review_questions.question: How does a provider differ from a vendor?
review_questions.answer: A provider operates cloud systems; a vendor sells products or services enabling cloud delivery.

review_questions.question: Which providers does the source name?
review_questions.answer: Google, Amazon/AWS, Yahoo!, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, HP, and SAP, among others.

review_questions.question: What does the article associate with AWS in 2002?
review_questions.answer: Amazon opened access to its systems through AWS on a utility-computing basis after data-center modernization.

review_questions.question: What idea does the source attribute to John McCarthy in 1960?
review_questions.answer: That computation might someday be organized as a public utility.

review_questions.question: Name some standards listed by the source.
review_questions.answer: HTTP, XMPP, OAuth, OpenID, SSL/TLS, Atom, AJAX, HTML5 offline, OVF, LAMP, XML, JSON, and REST.

review_questions.question: What was AGPL intended to address according to the source?
review_questions.answer: A perceived loophole involving modified free software run over a network.

review_questions.question: Why can managed services increase lock-in?
review_questions.answer: Applications may depend on provider-specific APIs, data models, identity systems, or operational behavior.

review_questions.question: What does a cloud dependency graph show?
review_questions.answer: How an application depends on compute, networks, storage, identity, databases, queues, and observability.

review_questions.question: Why are modern additions labeled synthesis?
review_questions.answer: They provide general architecture context not explicitly stated in the supplied historical article.
